idiom_name: asyncio.Queue mailbox + task loop (or queue.Queue + worker thread)
implementation_notes: Python's standard library ships no actor runtime, so the mailbox is hand-built: asyncio.Queue with maxsize (put/get await, put_nowait raising QueueFull) consumed by one long-lived task, or queue.Queue consumed by one dedicated thread when the actor must run blocking code. The actor is a plain class whose attributes are touched only by its consumer loop; Pykka and Ray are third-party wrappers over the same structure rather than a standard. Two limits decide the variant: asyncio gives concurrency, not parallelism, and on default CPython the GIL means thread actors do not run Python bytecode in parallel, so real CPU parallelism requires processes with pickled messages. The classic full structure is justified whenever handlers block or entities must be addressed; for one short-lived sequential operation, a coroutine or function is simpler.
pitfalls: asyncio.Queue is not thread-safe: a blocking actor needs queue.Queue and a real thread, and the two queues must never be mixed.
Without a sentinel or Queue.shutdown() the consumer task loops forever, so shutdown never completes cleanly.
The GIL makes thread-per-actor an illusion of parallelism for CPU-bound handlers; use processes or offload to native code.
An exception escaping the consumer task kills the actor silently unless the task is awaited or has a done-callback.
